briefing.text: Do not count raw rows in data_cna_hg19.seg as 'number of CNAs'. Many segments sit near seg.mean 0 and are not alterations. Call a segment altered only if |seg.mean| is above a log2 threshold (e.g. gain > 0.2, loss < -0.25, or |seg.mean| > 0.3). Exclude X/Y (and 23/24), and drop segments with very few markers (e.g. num.mark < 10). Compute both the count of altered segments and the fraction of genome altered (altered length / total covered autosomal length). Check that the comparison between lesions holds at thresholds 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, and with and without the small-segment filter.
briefing.reason: The headline metric depends on how a CNA is defined. Raw segment counts, or one arbitrary threshold, could reverse the comparison between lesions.

briefing.text: Samples are split into different numbers of segments, and neighbouring segments with the same direction inflate counts. Before counting, merge adjacent altered segments of the same direction within each chromosome. If the event count and the length-weighted fraction of genome altered disagree on which lesion has more CNAs, treat FGA as primary, because it is less sensitive to over-segmentation.
briefing.reason: Without this, differences in segmentation density between samples could pass for differences in CNA burden.

briefing.text: Before analysing, list sample IDs and lesion types from data_clinical_sample.txt and the seg file, and work out which patients have matched JP, DCIS and IDC samples. Possibly only one patient has all three, and the others are JP-only. The hypothesis is about JP versus its associated DCIS/IDC, so make the comparison within the matched patient(s) and describe it, rather than pooling unmatched samples. Use JP-only patients only as context for typical JP CNA levels. State that n is too small for a formal group test.
briefing.reason: This decides the comparison design and stops a pooled, unmatched test that misreads the word 'associated' in the hypothesis.

briefing.text: Take CNA burden from the copy-number segment file. Mutation counts or TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS measure point mutations and must not stand in for copy number alterations. At most, use them as side context.
briefing.reason: Stops the teams from swapping in the wrong variable for the one the hypothesis names.

briefing.text: Low tumour cell content (stroma-rich lesions) shrinks log2 ratios toward 0, so fixed thresholds under-call CNAs in low-purity samples. The clinical table may have no purity data; check. Report the spread of seg.mean per sample (e.g. SD and max |seg.mean|) next to the thresholded calls, and state purity as a caveat that cannot be corrected.
briefing.reason: Purity confounding can create or hide differences between lesions. Teams should report it, not ignore it.

briefing.text: Label logic: the hypothesis is directional (JP has high CNA burden compared with DCIS and IDC). If usable CNA data exist for the relevant lesions, the result is True or False depending on how JP ranks. 'Not verifiable' is right only if no relevant CNA variable or matched lesions exist. A small sample size alone does not make a claim unverifiable when the relevant measurement is present.
briefing.reason: Stops teams from defaulting to 'Not verifiable' because n is small when the data do contain the relevant variable.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat the seg.mean values of the five WXS samples as directly comparable in amplitude, so a fixed |seg.mean| threshold means the same thing in every sample. That holds only if tumour content and ploidy are similar, and neither team tested this.

Both teams equate 'number of CNAs' with fraction genome altered or with thresholded segment counts. The low-threshold event count is the one metric where team A saw JP ranked first. They called it noise but did not test that, for example against the noise in segments from the JP-only samples or by segment length.

Both teams take the single JuP3 trio as the whole test, and take JuP1/JuP2 only as context. Neither considered whether the hypothesis is about JP lesions as a class, meaning all three JP samples against the DCIS/IDC.
Team B does not say whether chromosome 23 (X) was excluded. Team A excluded it.
unused_evidence: data_mutations.txt has t_ref_count and t_alt_count. Variant allele fractions in each sample give an estimate of tumour content. Both teams said purity 'cannot be corrected', but this evidence is in the data. A low VAF in JuP3-JP would mean its flat CNA profile reflects low tumour content rather than few CNAs, and the comparison would then not settle the claim.
Mutations shared between JuP3-JP and JuP3-DCIS/IDC (the mutation file) show whether the JP is clonally related to them, which bears on what 'associated' means. Neither team checked this.

num.mark per segment and segment length. Team A filtered at num.mark>=10. Neither team looked at whether JP's extra low-amplitude segments at 0.1 are short and focal or broad, which would separate real subclonal or low-purity events from noise.
The clinical columns GRADE, ER, HER2 and TUMOR_SIZE are filled only for DCIS/IDC. This was not examined, though it is probably uninformative.
unresolved_weak_points: Purity. Both teams named low JP tumour content as their weakest point and only reported it. Neither used the VAF data that could test it.
Team A's own sign that JP has the most events at |seg.mean|>0.1 (18 vs 10/13) was resolved by choosing FGA as the primary measure, not by showing those events are noise.
With n=1 matched trio and no test, both teams' confidence of 0.8 is not justified by any stated uncertainty analysis.
second_readings: 'High number of copy number alterations' may mean a count of discrete events or breakpoints, not the fraction of the genome altered. Under a count reading at low amplitude thresholds, team A's data already rank JP first.
'JP' may mean JP lesions in general (JuP1, JuP2, JuP3-JP) compared with the DCIS/IDC associated with JP, not only the within-patient JuP3 comparison.

'Shows a high number' may be a claim about JP's genome being unstable at low amplitude (many small subclonal changes) once tumour content is accounted for. That would need amplitude scaled by purity, not raw log2 thresholds.
challenge.verdict: The direction looks consistent across FGA thresholds, so I moderately trust the agreed answer. But it rests on one trio, and both teams left the purity confound unaddressed even though VAF data in the mutation file could test it. Low JP tumour content could make a 'False' label really a 'cannot settle'.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: data_mutations.txt has t_ref_count and t_alt_count. Compute the median VAF of the mutations in JuP3-JP, JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC as a tumour-content proxy. If JP's tumour content is much lower, does a raw |seg.mean| threshold still support a definite label, or does it change your method or label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You called JP's 18 events at |seg.mean|>0.1 noise. Test that: compare their lengths, num.mark and amplitudes with the segments of the near-flat JuP1/JuP2 samples, and check whether they survive rescaling by a purity estimate. If they look like real low-amplitude events, does the 'number of CNAs' reading change your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Count the mutations JuP3-JP shares with JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC. Does the clonal relationship (related or independent lesions) change how you read 'associated DCIS and IDC', or how much weight the single-trio comparison can carry?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your weakest point is purity. Estimate tumour content for each JuP3 sample from t_alt_count/(t_ref_count+t_alt_count) in data_mutations.txt. If JP's VAFs are much lower than DCIS/IDC, does your threshold-based comparison still justify a definite label rather than a weaker one?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Did you exclude chromosome 23 (X) and filter short or low-num.mark segments? Re-run your counts with autosomes only and with a num.mark filter. Also report the plain number of discrete altered events (not FGA) at each threshold. Does any ranking flip for JP?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Compare all three JP samples (JuP1, JuP2, JuP3-JP) as a group with JuP3-DCIS/IDC, and check how many mutations JuP3-JP shares with its DCIS/IDC. Does reading 'JP' as the lesion class, or the evidence of clonal relatedness, change your method or confidence?

questions.why: Both teams named low purity as a confound but treated it as uncorrectable. If VAF-based purity adjustment is standard, the flat profile of the precursor lesion may be an artefact.

questions.question: In cancer genomics, when a paper reports a lesion as having a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually a count of discrete segments or breakpoints, or a genome-fraction metric? Which segment-mean thresholds are conventional for calling gains and losses from exome-derived segmentation?
questions.why: In this data the ranking depends on whether the count or the fraction reading is used, and on the threshold.

findings.question: How does tumour purity (normal-cell contamination) affect log2 copy-ratio segment means from exome sequencing? What are the standard ways to adjust copy-number burden metrics such as fraction genome altered for purity, for example by estimating purity from somatic variant allele fractions?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on all 4 calls, so this comes from domain knowledge only. Normal-cell contamination pulls log2 ratios toward 0. The observed ratio is about (p*C + 2(1-p)) / (p*ploidy + 2(1-p)), so at purity 0.3 a one-copy loss is about -0.23 and a one-copy gain about +0.20, close to typical calling thresholds. Standard practice is to estimate purity (ABSOLUTE, ASCAT, FACETS, Sequenza, PureCN, or roughly 2x the median VAF of clonal heterozygous somatic SNVs in copy-neutral regions) and then rescale log2 ratios before thresholding and computing FGA (e.g. CNVkit call --purity). VAF-based purity needs enough somatic mutations to be reliable, so for a low-TMB lesion it is weak. Purity is therefore a real and partly correctable confound, but with sparse mutations it stays a caveat rather than a dependable adjustment.

findings.question: In cancer genomics, when a paper reports a lesion as having a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually a count of discrete segments or breakpoints, or a genome-fraction metric? Which segment-mean thresholds are conventional for calling gains and losses from exome-derived segmentation?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the gateway returned HTTP 403, so this comes from domain knowledge only. Papers use both readings: a count of altered segments or events, or a genome fraction (FGA or percent genome altered). Which one is meant has to be checked case by case, so robust analyses report both. Conventional log2 thresholds: cBioPortal FGA uses |seg.mean| > 0.2; CNVkit call defaults are -1.1/-0.25/+0.2/+0.7; GATK CallCopyRatioSegments treats copy ratio 0.9-1.1 (log2 about -0.15/+0.14) as neutral; GISTIC uses a noise threshold of 0.1; ±0.3 is common for noisy exome data. The ranking should be checked to hold across thresholds of 0.1-0.3.
